title: Which Entrance Did You Mean?
scene: You're meeting a friend at a weekend art market. The venue has two entrances, so a quick clarification saves you from waiting in different places.
sceneJa: 週末のアートマーケットで友人と待ち合わせ。会場には入口が二つあるのに、友人の連絡は「入口で待ってる」だけ。早合点せず確認し、位置情報を送ってすれ違いを防ぐ場面。

chunks.en: We agreed to meet at the weekend art market,
chunks.ja: 週末のアートマーケットで待ち合わせることにしたが
入口が二つ載っていた

chunks.en: Aya texted, 'I'll wait by the entrance,'
chunks.ja: アヤから「入口で待ってるね」と連絡が来て
僕はもう少しでそのまま向かうところだった
どちらの入口か確かめずに
念のため確認しようと

chunks.en: I replied, 'Do you mean the one by the station
chunks.ja: 「駅側の入口のこと？ と返信した

chunks.en: or the one next to the park?'
chunks.ja: それとも公園の隣の入口？」と

chunks.en: She wrote back, 'The one by the park—
chunks.ja: 彼女は「公園側のほうだよ」と返して
「もっとはっきり伝えるべきだったね」と付け加えた

chunks.en: I sent her a map pin
chunks.ja: 僕は地図上の位置情報を送った
そうすれば〜ということにならずに済むように
別々の場所で待ち続けることに

chunks.en: We found each other in minutes,
chunks.ja: 僕らは数分で無事に合流できた
それは珍しくうれしい変化だった
いつもの『どこにいる？』と探り合う待ち合わせに比べれば

questions.question: Which chunking keeps the speaker's clarification together naturally?
options: Just to / make sure I replied / Do you mean the one / by the station or / the one next to the park?
Just to make sure / I replied, 'Do you mean the one by the station / or the one next to the park?'
Just to make / sure I replied, Do / you mean the one by / the station or the one next / to the park?
questions.explanation: ‘Just to make sure’ is a natural introductory phrase. Keep the two alternative entrances together as a clear either-or question.

questions.question: What does ‘I should've been more specific’ mean here?
options: I should have arrived at the market earlier.
I should have changed our meeting day.
I should have said exactly which entrance I meant.
questions.explanation: ‘Should've’ means ‘should have’. Aya is acknowledging that ‘the entrance’ was too vague because there were two.

questions.question: Why does the narrator send a map pin after Aya clarifies?
options: To make the meeting point unmistakable and avoid waiting in different places.
To suggest moving the meeting to another day.
To show Aya a different art market.
questions.explanation: The pin confirms the precise location. The narrator is preventing a small but common misunderstanding.

speak: Imagine meeting someone at a venue with more than one entrance. Round 1: Read ‘Just to make sure / I replied, “Do you mean the one by the station / or the one next to the park?”’ slowly, pausing at the slashes. Round 2: Stress ‘station’ and ‘park’ to make the choice clear; soften ‘Just to make sure’ so it sounds helpful rather than suspicious. Round 3: Read the six sentences as a short, lightly amused story. Then speak for 30 seconds: Where are you meeting? What is unclear? Ask ‘Just to make sure, do you mean ...?’ and explain how you'll confirm the spot. Final Read: Read all six sentences again without looking at the Japanese.
review: Reuse expressions in a different situation. Lesson 91: ‘I almost ...’ (もう少しで〜するところだった) described nearly skipping a walk; here, ‘I almost headed over’ describes nearly going to an unclear meeting point. Lesson 80: ‘end up ...’ (結局〜することになる) described an unintended result in a work process; here, ‘end up waiting in different places’ is a social mix-up to avoid. New chunks: ‘Just to make sure’ (念のため), ‘Do you mean ...?’ (〜という意味？), and ‘I should've been more specific’ (もっと具体的に伝えるべきだった).
